subtopics.title: Constitution and Role of the Commission
subtopics.summary: The 16th Finance Commission was set up in 2023 under Article 280 to recommend how tax revenue is distributed between the Centre and the States. It has one Chairperson, Dr. Arvind Panagariya, and four other members, appointed by the President for a generally five-year tenure. Its report and an Action Taken Memorandum are laid before Parliament under Article 281, and the Government has accepted its key recommendations for 2026-31.

subtopics.title: Vertical and Horizontal Devolution
subtopics.summary: Vertical devolution fixes the share of the Centre's divisible tax pool transferred to the States, which the 16th Commission kept at 41 per cent. Horizontal devolution decides how that 41 per cent is divided among States, and the revised criteria add GDP contribution while reducing the weight of income distance and geographical area. The divisible pool excludes cesses, surcharges and the cost of collection.

subtopics.title: Grants-in-Aid, Cess and Surcharge
subtopics.summary: Statutory grants under Article 275 go only to States in need of financial assistance and are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India every year. Discretionary grants under Article 282 can be made for any public purpose, and the Centre has no obligation to give them. Cesses and surcharges are levied by the Centre and are not shared with States, while SASCI provides long-term interest-free loans for capital projects.

subtopics.title: Fiscal Discipline and Local Bodies
subtopics.summary: The Commission recommends that the Centre's fiscal deficit fall to 3.5 per cent of GDP and the States' limit be set at 3 per cent of GSDP by 2030-31. It also recommends ending off-budget borrowings by States and performance-linked grants for local bodies. For urban areas it proposes an urbanisation premium and a constitutional change regarding State Finance Commission recommendations.

subtopics.title: Impact, Concerns and Past Commissions
subtopics.summary: The retained 41 per cent share is said to give States revenue predictability, and the revised formula is said to safeguard fiscally weaker States. Critics point to the 41 per cent share falling short of the 50 per cent demanded, the reduced weight for demographic performance, and the discontinuation of revenue-deficit grants. Finance Commissions have been appointed since 1951, and the early chairpersons include K.C. Neogy.

quizzes.passage: The 16th Finance Commission's recommendations for 2026-31 shape how tax revenue is shared between the Centre and the States. The first stage of sharing is vertical devolution, which fixes the overall share of the Centre's divisible tax pool that States receive. The Commission has kept this share at 41 per cent, the same level set by the previous Commission. The divisible pool covers the Centre's gross tax revenues but leaves out cesses, surcharges and the cost of collection. States have raised concerns that these levies are kept by the Union and not shared, which reduces the untied fiscal space available to them. The second stage is horizontal devolution, which decides how the 41 per cent share is apportioned among individual States. The revised criteria add contribution to GDP as a new parameter, while income distance and geographical area are given less weight. Demographic performance also receives less weight, which has raised fears of an 'Ageing Before Prosperity' problem in some Southern States. The package also seeks fiscal discipline, with the Commission proposing deficit limits for both the Centre and the States by 2030-31. Together, these measures aim to balance fiscal federalism, equity and economic performance.

quizzes.passage: The Commission's recommendations also reach beyond the Union and State governments to local bodies, which deliver services at the grassroots level. It recommends grants for both rural and urban local bodies and for disaster management, and it links part of these grants to performance so that local bodies are held accountable. To encourage the growth of cities, it proposes a premium that rewards the merger of neighbouring peri-urban villages into adjoining urban local bodies, provided the receiving body has a population above a set level. The report also suggests removing a constitutional requirement that Central Finance Commission recommendations be made on the basis of State Finance Commission recommendations. On fiscal matters, the Commission wants the Centre and the States to keep their deficits within set limits by a target year, and it has recommended ending off-budget borrowings by States so that debt is transparent. Some borrowing for capital investment through a long-term, interest-free loan scheme is kept outside the deficit limit. The Commission also urged States to pursue reforms in power distribution companies and to use targeted subsidies that come with sunset clauses.
